Mixed Effect Model Tutorial

Sleep Health Analytics Resource Center

26 June, 2026

This tutorial is for running mixed effect models in R.

We will use the R packages lme4 and lmerTest. The package nlme also performs mixed effect models. For more information see https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlme/nlme.pdf

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(tidyverse)
library(sjPlot)
library(knitr)
library(performance)
library(broom.mixed)
library(table1)

Our study consists of 100 adolescents whom we want to study their sleep and mood over a maximum of 10 years follow up.

# GENERATE SAMPLE DATA SET

#set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1212) 
# set number of people
n_people <- 100

# create dataframe for IDs with ID number, sex, sleep dx, screen use, and random number of visits between 1 and 10
people <- data.frame(
  id  = 1:n_people,
  sex = sample(c("M", "F"), n_people, replace = TRUE),
  sleep_dx = sample(c("1", "0"), n_people, replace = TRUE),
  ses = sample(c(1:10), n_people, replace = TRUE),
  n_visits = sample(1:10, n_people, replace = TRUE), 
  age_bl = sample(10:15, n_people, replace = TRUE),
  base_duration = runif(n_people, min = 4, max = 11),  # person-specific mean, 
  slope = runif(n_people, min = -0.6, max = -0.1)      
)

# create time varying data with duration and mood
long_data <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:n_people, function(i) {
  n_i <- people$n_visits[i]
  visits <- 1:n_i
  
 
   duration_i <- if (people$sleep_dx[i] == 0) {
        # Stable duration for no sleep dx
        people$base_duration[i] + rnorm(n_i, mean = 0, sd = 1)
      } else {
        # Decreasing duration over time for sleep dx
        people$base_duration[i] +
          people$slope[i] * (visits - 1) +
          rnorm(n_i, mean = 0, sd = 1)
      }
   
    # Enforce bounds
    duration_i <- pmin(pmax(duration_i, 3), 12)

    # Mood correlated with duration
    # Linear relationship + noise
    mood_i <- 3 + 0.5 * duration_i + rnorm(n_i, sd = 2)
    mood_i <- pmin(pmax(mood_i, 1), 10)

  
    
    data.frame(
      id = people$id[i],
      visit = 1:n_i,
      sex = people$sex[i],
      sleep_dx = people$sleep_dx[i],
      ses = people$ses[i],
      duration = duration_i,  
      mood = mood_i,
      age = people$age_bl[i] + 1:n_i -1,
      age_bl = people$age_bl[i]
    )
  })
)

# sort by id and visit
long_data <- long_data[order(long_data$id, long_data$visit), ]

We have basic demographic information at baseline: age, sex, sleep disorder diagnosis, and SES (1-10 scale).

At each visit we have mood (1-10 scale), sleep duration (hours), and age at follow up.

What is a mixed effect model and how does it work?

An assumption of a basic linear regression model is that all observations are independent.

ggplot(data = subset(long_data, id < 16), aes(x = age, y = duration)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = .25) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  xlab("Age") + 
  ylab("Sleep duration") +
  ggtitle("Sleep and Age")+
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

When we have repeated data across participants this assumption no longer holds because observations from the same person may be more highly correlated than observations from different people.

ggplot(data = subset(long_data, id < 16), aes(x = age, y = duration)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = .75, aes(color = as.factor(id))) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_discrete("ID")+
  xlab("Age") + 
  ylab("Sleep duration") +
  ggtitle("Sleep and Age")+
  theme_bw()

Additionally data that is collected across multiple groups, sites, or sometimes days violates this assumption because observations within the group are likely more highly correlated than observations outside the group.

Mixed effect models allow us to group dependent measurements like those from the same person/group.

Fixed Effects and Random Effects

Mixed effect models are composed of fixed effects and random effects.

Think of fixed effects as the overall estimates we want to get from our model: our predictor and covariates.

The random effects are additional specifications we give the model explaining how to structure the data. Mixed effect models generally consists of random intercepts and random slopes.

In the following equation:

Yij = B0 + B1*xij + B2*xi + b0i + b1i*μij + εij

εij = σ20i + σ21ij

i = person level

j = observation level

The fixed effects are:

  • B0 ~ global intercept
  • B1*xij ~ time varying predictor (age, time in study, predictor measured over time)
  • B2*xi ~ time invarying predictor (baseline demographics, baseline predictors)

The random effects are:

  • b0i ~ random intercept
  • b1i*μij ~ random slope on our time-varying predictor

The error terms are:

  • σ20i ~ random effect variance (variance between groups)
  • σ21ij ~ residual variance (variance within group)

Building a Mixed Effect Model

To start, we might ask the question, does sleep duration change on average over the follow up?

ggplot(data = long_data, aes(x = visit, y = duration, color = factor(id), group = factor(id))) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = .25) +
  xlab("Years in study") + 
  ylab("Sleep duration") +
  ggtitle("Spaghetti plot")+
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

We can build a model with sleep duration as our outcome, and visit number as our predictor.

Random Intercept

Here we specify a random intercept by id using the code (1|id) to tell the model that there is more than 1 observation per id and to group by id.

fit1 <- lmer(duration ~ visit + (1 |id), data = long_data)
summary(fit1)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: duration ~ visit + (1 | id)
##    Data: long_data
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 1936.9
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -2.89106 -0.59998 -0.02648  0.63664  2.70345 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
##  id       (Intercept) 4.247    2.061   
##  Residual             1.082    1.040   
## Number of obs: 562, groups:  id, 100
## 
## Fixed effects:
##              Estimate Std. Error        df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   7.67468    0.22362 119.02175  34.321   <2e-16 ***
## visit        -0.18267    0.01922 479.97096  -9.503   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##       (Intr)
## visit -0.292

To answer our question, does sleep duration change on average over the follow up?

Yes, sleep duration is decreasing over time. To interpret the B coefficient we can say: Each year the sleep duration is decreasing by 0.18 hours on average.

To visualize the global trend of our model we can plot it using the plot_model function in sjPlot

plot_model(fit1, type = "pred") + 
  theme_bw()

Behind the scenes our model fits each individual with their own beta intercept which we can extract and plot!

#extract random intercepts per id
random_int <- ranef(fit1)$id # this is how far the intercept differs from the global intercept
random_int$id = as.numeric(row.names(random_int))
#join random intercepts with data set
long_data_r_int <- long_data %>%
  full_join(random_int, by = join_by(id))%>%
  mutate(adj_random_int = `(Intercept)` + fit1@beta[1], # adjust random intercepts from global intercept. 
         fit.c = predict(fit1, re.form = NULL))# get fitted values for each individual line at all points
head(long_data_r_int) %>%kable()
id visit sex sleep_dx ses duration mood age age_bl (Intercept) adj_random_int fit.c
1 1 F 1 7 6.594244 3.954897 11 11 -1.177929 6.496749 6.314076
1 2 F 1 7 5.502200 5.644387 12 11 -1.177929 6.496749 6.131402
1 3 F 1 7 7.257461 10.000000 13 11 -1.177929 6.496749 5.948729
1 4 F 1 7 7.387598 5.569759 14 11 -1.177929 6.496749 5.766055
1 5 F 1 7 5.623388 6.422468 15 11 -1.177929 6.496749 5.583381
1 6 F 1 7 5.281096 6.049538 16 11 -1.177929 6.496749 5.400708 
ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = long_data_r_int, aes(x = visit, y = duration, col = factor(id), group = factor(id)), size = 1, alpha = .75) +
  geom_line(data = long_data_r_int, aes(x = visit, y = fit.c, col = factor(id)), size = 1.5, alpha = .5) +
  geom_abline(intercept = fit1@beta[1], slope = fit1@beta[2], color = "black", size = 2) +
  xlab("Years in study") + 
  ylab("Sleep duration") +
  ggtitle("Predicted duration over time with random intercept")+
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Here we see that mixed effect models can handle different amounts of follow up. Some people have only 1 visit and others have all 10. However, your hypothesis may warrant filtering our participants hwo do not meet a certain threshold.

Random Intercept and Slope

Additionally, we can specify a random slope using the code (1 + visit |id) to tell the model that each line can also have its own slope based on that individual’s sleep duration trajectory over time.

fit1.1 <- lmer(duration ~ visit + (1 + visit |id), data = long_data)
summary(fit1.1)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: duration ~ visit + (1 + visit | id)
##    Data: long_data
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 1890.2
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -2.30506 -0.61201  0.04738  0.59134  2.49465 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr 
##  id       (Intercept) 4.5221   2.1265        
##           visit       0.0374   0.1934   -0.23
##  Residual             0.8522   0.9232        
## Number of obs: 562, groups:  id, 100
## 
## Fixed effects:
##             Estimate Std. Error       df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  7.63632    0.22822 99.19203  33.461  < 2e-16 ***
## visit       -0.16612    0.03086 58.96220  -5.384 1.33e-06 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##       (Intr)
## visit -0.348

We still see a similar result that…

Yes, sleep duration is (still) decreasing over time. To interpret the B coefficient we can say: Each year the sleep duration is decreasing by 0.17 hours on average.

For this model, we can extract not only an individual B intercept, but also an individual slope per person.

#extract random intercepts per id
random_int <- ranef(fit1.1)$id # this is how far the intercept/slope differs from the fixed intercept/slope
colnames(random_int)[colnames(random_int) == 'visit'] <- 'visit_random'
random_int$id = as.numeric(row.names(random_int))

#join random intercepts with data set
long_data_r_int <- long_data %>%
  full_join(random_int, by = join_by(id))%>%
  mutate(adj_random_int = `(Intercept)` + fit1.1@beta[1], # adjust random intercepts from the fixed intercept
         adj_random_slope_visit = visit_random + fit1.1@beta[2],# adjust random slope from fixed intercept
         fit.c = predict(fit1.1, re.form = NULL))# get fitted values for each individual line at all points
head(long_data_r_int)%>%kable()

ggplot()+
  geom_point(data = long_data_r_int, aes(x = visit, y = duration, col = factor(id), group = factor(id)), size = 1, alpha = .75) +
  geom_line(data = long_data_r_int, aes(x = visit, y = fit.c, col = factor(id)), size = 2, alpha = .5) +
  geom_abline(intercept = fit1.1@beta[1], slope = fit1.1@beta[2], color = "black", size = 2) +
  xlab("Years in study") + 
  ylab("Sleep duration") +
  ggtitle("Predicted duration over time with random intercept and random slope")+
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Output

Now let’s interpret the output we get from the summary() and tab_model() functions.

summary(fit1.1)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: duration ~ visit + (1 + visit | id)
##    Data: long_data
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 1890.2
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -2.30506 -0.61201  0.04738  0.59134  2.49465 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr 
##  id       (Intercept) 4.5221   2.1265        
##           visit       0.0374   0.1934   -0.23
##  Residual             0.8522   0.9232        
## Number of obs: 562, groups:  id, 100
## 
## Fixed effects:
##             Estimate Std. Error       df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  7.63632    0.22822 99.19203  33.461  < 2e-16 ***
## visit       -0.16612    0.03086 58.96220  -5.384 1.33e-06 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

tab_model(fit1.1)
  duration
Predictors Estimates CI p
(Intercept) 7.64 7.19 – 8.08 <0.001
visit -0.17 -0.23 – -0.11 <0.001
Random Effects
σ2 0.85
τ00 id 4.52
τ11 id.visit 0.04
ρ01 id -0.23
ICC 0.84
N id 100
Observations 562
Marginal R2 / Conditional R2 0.033 / 0.850

σ2 = residual variance (the within person variability)

τ00 = variance of random intercept

τ11 = variance of random slope

ρ01 = correlation between random intercept and slope (the amount of covariance between intercept and slope is due to their shared variation)

ICC = is the proportion of the variance explained by the grouping structure in the population:

Remember our error terms we specified above?

Error:

  • σ20i ~ random effect variance (variance between groups)
  • σ21ij ~ residual variance (variance within group)

ICC = σ20i / (σ20i + σ21ij)

Low ICC:

An ICC close to 0 (or <0.4) indicates that most of the variability is within person and within person measurements are not more highly correlated compared to measurements from other people. This may provide evidence that a mixed effect framework is not need, however with repeated measures from the same person, a mixed effect model is strongly advised.

High ICC:

An ICC close to 1 indicates that most of the variability is between person. This provides evidence that the mixed effect framework is necessary.

From the performance package you can calculate it using the function icc().

icc(fit1.1)
## # Intraclass Correlation Coefficient
## 
##     Adjusted ICC: 0.844
##   Unadjusted ICC: 0.817

Usually we care about the adjusted ICC.

N = number of participants

Marginal R2 = the amount of variance explained by the fixed effects

Conditional R2 = the amount of variance explained by the fixed and random effect.

Usually we care about the conditional R2.

Interactions in Mixed effect Models

Sometimes we are interested in how one variable affects another variable’s relationship with the outcome. In psychology we often call this moderation.

Below are some examples of when to add interactions and how to interpret the B coefficients.

Time interaction

Does the change in sleep duration over the follow up differ between those with and without a sleep disorder diagnosis?

What we are asking mathematically is, Is there a difference in the slope of duration over time in between the sleep diagnosis groups?

ggplot(data = long_data, aes(x = visit, y = duration, color = sleep_dx, group = factor(id))) + 
  geom_line() + 
  theme_bw() 

fit2 <- lmer(duration ~ visit + sleep_dx + sex + visit*sleep_dx +(1 + visit |id), data = long_data)
summary(fit2)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: duration ~ visit + sleep_dx + sex + visit * sleep_dx + (1 + visit |  
##     id)
##    Data: long_data
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 1857.4
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -2.73196 -0.60332  0.04712  0.59659  2.48559 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr 
##  id       (Intercept) 4.74915  2.1793        
##           visit       0.01294  0.1138   -0.54
##  Residual             0.86661  0.9309        
## Number of obs: 562, groups:  id, 100
## 
## Fixed effects:
##                  Estimate Std. Error        df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)       7.69847    0.35664 103.79869  21.586  < 2e-16 ***
## visit            -0.01639    0.03205  58.50092  -0.511    0.611    
## sleep_dx1         0.47035    0.46911  97.69280   1.003    0.319    
## sexM             -0.67641    0.41749  94.21553  -1.620    0.109    
## visit:sleep_dx1  -0.30725    0.04495  54.72681  -6.835 7.18e-09 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##             (Intr) visit  slp_d1 sexM  
## visit       -0.438                     
## sleep_dx1   -0.574  0.332              
## sexM        -0.409  0.003 -0.143       
## vst:slp_dx1  0.319 -0.713 -0.472 -0.018

Yes! Those with a sleep diagnosis have a 0.31 hour decrease on average in duration per year compared to those without a sleep diagnosis.

Notice our model has a:

  • random slope for visit, allowing the slope of duration to change over time
  • random intercept by id, grouping all observations from
  • covariate for sex

Let’s visualize the interaction:

plot_model(fit2, type = "int") + 
  theme_bw()

The graph shows us that those with a sleep disorder diagnosis have a decreasing duration over time and those with no sleep disorder have constant sleep over time.

Note: the coefficient tells us about the DIFFERENCE in slopes, but the graph tells us the direction of the change.

2 Categorical Interaction

Do sleep disorders have a greater affect on duration for female participants compared to male?

fit3 <- lmer(duration ~ visit + sleep_dx + sex + sex*sleep_dx +(1 + visit |id), data = long_data)
summary(fit3)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: duration ~ visit + sleep_dx + sex + sex * sleep_dx + (1 + visit |  
##     id)
##    Data: long_data
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 1882.7
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max

Separating Within and Between Person Effects

Cross sectional models

Now we are interested in the relationship between duration and mood, which are both measured at each time point.

We can plot mood over time by id.

ggplot(data = long_data, aes(x = visit, y = mood, color = factor(id), group = factor(id))) + 
  geom_line() + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

We can plot the relationship between duration and mood by id

ggplot(data = long_data, aes(x = duration, y = mood, color = factor(id), group = factor(id))) + 
  geom_line() + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

It looks like mood and duration are related, so we can test that using a mixed effect model.

fit6 <- lmer(mood ~ duration + sleep_dx + sex + visit + (1 + duration |id), data = long_data)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
summary(fit6)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: mood ~ duration + sleep_dx + sex + visit + (1 + duration | id)
##    Data: long_data
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 2314.9
##

## -2.86480 -0.68645  0.01279  0.71193  2.71929 
## 
## Random effects:

##  id       (Intercept) 0.9372   0.9681        
##           duration    0.0110   0.1049   -1.00
##  Residual             3.4309   1.8523        
## Number of obs: 562, groups:  id, 100
## 
## Fixed effects:
##              Estimate Std. Error        df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   2.76446    0.38348 163.33262   7.209 1.98e-11 ***
## duration      0.48428    0.03945 142.80561  12.275  < 2e-16 ***
## sleep_dx1    -0.06055    0.17737 209.73055  -0.341   0.7332    
## sexM          0.23866    0.17788 186.63782   1.342   0.1813    
## visit         0.06062    0.03138 545.56079   1.932   0.0539 .  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

##           (Intr) duratn slp_d1 sexM  
## duration  -0.882                     
## sleep_dx1 -0.341  0.190              
## sexM      -0.270  0.150 -0.181       
## visit     -0.472  0.170  0.043 -0.006
## optimizer (nloptwrap) convergence code: 0 (OK)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')

Notice, we also get a warning, boundary (singular) fit: see help(‘isSingular’). This tells us that the model is over fitted and we may have too many random effects. Essentially there is not a big enough difference in one of the random effects across all the ids to be necessary in the model.

Let’s refit the model without the random slope.

fit6 <- lmer(mood ~ duration + sleep_dx + sex + visit + (1 |id), data = long_data)
summary(fit6)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: mood ~ duration + sleep_dx + sex + visit + (1 | id)
##    Data: long_data
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: 2318.6
##

## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
##  id       (Intercept) 0.04934  0.2221  
##  Residual             3.50392  1.8719  
## Number of obs: 562, groups:  id, 100

## Fixed effects:
##              Estimate Std. Error        df t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   2.79375    0.36324 169.97778   7.691 1.12e-12 ***
## duration      0.48500    0.03734 138.62788  12.989  < 2e-16 ***
## sleep_dx1    -0.04217    0.17391  85.73513  -0.243   0.8090    
## sexM          0.14398    0.17276  79.65894   0.833   0.4071    
## visit         0.05837    0.03130 546.07218   1.865   0.0627 .  
## ---

## sexM      -0.278  0.152 -0.162       
## visit     -0.505  0.194  0.024 -0.003

When we run it again without the random slope, the warning goes away.

So what do the results tell us?

As AVERAGE duration increases, so does AVERAGE mood.

But, this does NOT tell us if that change is happening within person or between person. To do this, we must separate out the within and between person effects.

long_data_within_btwn <- long_data %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(btwn_dur = mean(duration),  # mean duration for each person (repeated over time)
         wthin_dur = duration - btwn_dur) # individual's deviation from the mean

head(long_data_within_btwn) %>%kable()
id visit sex sleep_dx ses duration mood age age_bl btwn_dur wthin_dur
1 1 F 1 7 6.594244 3.954897 11 11 5.550039 1.0442044
1 2 F 1 7 5.502200 5.644387 12 11 5.550039 -0.0478388
1 3 F 1 7 7.257461 10.000000 13 11 5.550039 1.7074213
1 4 F 1 7 7.387598 5.569759 14 11 5.550039 1.8375584
1 5 F 1 7 5.623388 6.422468 15 11 5.550039 0.0733489
1 6 F 1 7 5.281096 6.049538 16 11 5.550039 -0.2689434

Between person is a repeated measure of the average and within person is the deviation from that average.

fit6.1 <- lmer(mood ~ wthin_dur + btwn_dur + sleep_dx + sex + visit + (1 |id), data = long_data_within_btwn)
summary(fit6.1)

Between person: For every 1 hour on average that some sleeps compared to their peer, the mood score increases by 0.47.

Predictive models

With longitudinal data, we can reformat the data to predict a future outcome. Here we pair current sleep with next year’s mood.

# reformat data to pair depression with next years mood.
mood_next_year <- long_data_within_btwn %>%
  select(id, visit, mood)%>%
  mutate(visit_cs = visit, # cross sectional visit
         visit = visit - 1,
         mood_next_year = mood) %>%
  select( - mood)
long_data_pred <- full_join(long_data_within_btwn, mood_next_year, by = join_by(id, visit))

head(long_data_pred) %>% kable()
id visit sex sleep_dx ses duration mood age age_bl btwn_dur wthin_dur visit_cs mood_next_year

1 5 F 1 7 5.623388 6.422468 15 11 5.550039 0.0733489 6 6.049538
1 6 F 1 7 5.281096 6.049538 16 11 5.550039 -0.2689434 7 7.003266 
fit7 <- lmer(mood_next_year ~ wthin_dur + btwn_dur + mood +  (1 |id), data = long_data_pred)
summary(fit7)

Other distributions

When we have other types of outcomes, we can use other distributions to model the data.

#create new data
long_data_dist <- long_data_within_btwn  %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    site = sample(c("home", "lab"), size = 1)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    # Add a negative intercept to lower overall probability
    prob_depression = plogis(-2 + (-0.8 * scale(mood))),
    
    depression = rbinom(n(), size = 1, prob = prob_depression),
    
    MH_count = pmin(rpois(n(), lambda = 3), 13)
  ) %>%
  select(-prob_depression)
head(long_data_dist) %>% kable()
id visit sex sleep_dx ses duration mood age age_bl btwn_dur wthin_dur site depression MH_count
1 1 F 1 7 6.594244 3.954897 11 11 5.550039 1.0442044 lab 1 2
1 2 F 1 7 5.502200 5.644387 12 11 5.550039 -0.0478388 lab 0 2
1 3 F 1 7 7.257461 10.000000 13 11 5.550039 1.7074213 lab 0 2
1 4 F 1 7 7.387598 5.569759 14 11 5.550039 1.8375584 lab 0 3
1 5 F 1 7 5.623388 6.422468 15 11 5.550039 0.0733489 lab 1 4
1 6 F 1 7 5.281096 6.049538 16 11 5.550039 -0.2689434 lab 1 1

If we expand our study to include an measure for depression indicator and mental health risk count at each time point, we can explore mixed effect models with other distributions

Logistic

When we have a binary outcome, like depression here, we can use a logistic regression model with the glmer function. This runs a generalized linear mixed effect model, where the family indicates the distribution.

fit8 <- glmer(depression ~ wthin_dur + btwn_dur + sex + (1 |id), family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = long_data_dist)
summary(fit8)
## Generalized linear mixed model fit by maximum likelihood (Laplace
##   Approximation) [glmerMod]
##  Family: binomial  ( logit )
## Formula: depression ~ wthin_dur + btwn_dur + sex + (1 | id)
##    Data: long_data_dist
##

##     488.9     510.5    -239.4     478.9       557 
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -0.6864 -0.4420 -0.3753 -0.3190  3.1766 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups Name        Variance Std.Dev.
##  id     (Intercept) 0.2398   0.4897  
## Number of obs: 562, groups:  id, 100
## 
## Fixed effects:
##             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)  
## (Intercept) -0.70217    0.48768  -1.440   0.1499  
## wthin_dur   -0.13527    0.11475  -1.179   0.2385  
## btwn_dur    -0.14602    0.06511  -2.243   0.0249 *
## sexM        -0.16284    0.27293  -0.597   0.5507  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

## wthin_dur  0.007              
## btwn_dur  -0.927  0.016       
## sexM      -0.427  0.013  0.220

Because logistic models use a logit link, the B coefficients need to exponentiated to be interpretable.

eB

We can do this with the tidy() function, or the tab_model() function.

tidy(fit8, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE, effects = "fixed")

tab_model(fit8)

Poisson/Negative Binomial

When we have a count outcome, like mental health risk, we can use either a Poisson or Negative Binomial regression model.

From Poisson, neither within or between person duration is significant. We could interpret it as for every one hour increase in within person duration, there is a 1% decrease in the risk of MH count increasing by 1.

Negative Binomial

fit9.1 <- glmer.nb(MH_count ~ wthin_dur + btwn_dur  + (1 |id), data = long_data_dist)

The negative binomial model has singularity/convergence issues.

LRT

The likelihood ratio tests if Poisson or negative binomial models are better for the data.

p <- pchisq(2 * (logLik(fit9.1) - logLik(fit9)), df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
t <- ifelse(p > 0.05, "Poisson is better", "NB is better" )
print(t)
## [1] "Poisson is better"

This result is confirmed by the fact that our negative binomial model has convergence issues.

For more information on deciding between negative binomial or poisson, see the link below:

https://www.statology.org/negative-binomial-vs-poisson/

Interactions

Instead of testing for a difference in slopes, other distributions test for an difference in odds ratios (logistic) or a difference in risk ratios (poisson/NB).

Multilevel nesting

Sometimes we may want to nest our groups on multiple levels. For example in this data set we have a site variable that indicates that indicates if the measurements were taken at home or in a lab. We may expect all data collected in the lab to be more similar compared to data collected at home.

We can nest by site and id with the notation (1 | site/id) or (1 | site + id). This will create a random intercept for each id and collectively across the sites.

fit10 <- lmer(mood ~ wthin_dur + btwn_dur + visit + (1  | site/id), data = long_data_dist)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
summary(fit10)

However, our model gives a singularity warning. The model is over-fitted meaning that some variance components equal zero. This can happen when we specify a random effect. This may mean that it is best to simplify the model by removing some random effects, like site.

fit10.1 <- lmer(mood ~ wthin_dur + btwn_dur + visit + (1  | id), data = long_data_dist)
summary(fit10.1)
